4 unchanged paragraphs, under Version 0.2: what it cost, and what it keeps earning

[figure collage-views.webp] The vault, view by view: twenty of its twenty-two views, the nine new in version 0.2 outlined.

**Costs and profit.** The fixed cost is mostly the reporting, and it comes first: 50 hours of the reporter's time and 7.5 of the editor's, £2,040 with a legal read, set-up and the platform. The variable costs, payments, alerts, compute and hosting, follow use and come to 9.3% of revenue. During the closure the Courier makes £678, the infrastructure share covers its costs with £20 to spare, and the reporter is under water: her share is about £19 an hour against a cost basis of £30. The story breaks even on 20 November, day forty, and the scale chart says why the town mattered: below about 1,500 followers it would not have paid for its reporting, and above that every follower is margin.

[figure el-economics-charts.webp] Revenue against cost, day by day, crossing on 20 November; and the same story with more or fewer followers, where fixed costs stay put and variable costs follow use.

**Two years on.** The story stopped being news on 4 December. It kept selling. A council post-incident review, loss adjusters handling business-interruption claims, the county's inspections of eight bridges of the same design, a second fund ahead of the contractor's results, a procurement watchdog, a university research group, an insurer and two other towns with the same bridge all buy the record of what was known, when, and from whom. Over two years the bridge earns £4,378 and £1,181 of profit. After the reopening, 96% of its revenue comes from institutions and agents rather than the town: the revenue moves from the local reader to the players who want the data. The reporter's effective rate rises from £20 an hour at the reopening to £25.54, and Priya's three photographs have earned her £328.

[figure el-projection-chart.webp] Revenue by month over two years, by who paid: the town in October and November, institutions and agents after that, against a cost that is almost all in the first two months.

**The next stories, and the payment as a signal.** The bridge is the first story in the Courier's graph, not the last. The vault plays out eleven more over two years: a school catchment change, the footbridge resurfacing, the county's sister-bridge inspections, a business rates review, a bus timetable, a wharf flood-defence overrun, a contractor's pattern across three councils, a car park, winter floods, a school meals contract and night closures on the bypass. Each starts with the council, the procurement portal, the routes and the contributors already in the graph, which saves 157 of 331 reporting hours. And each is sized by what people paid for in its first week, from readers and from institutions asking ahead: six are investigated, five get a tracker, and the footbridge resurfacing, which few people needed, gets a brief, three hours and a £73 loss that keeps the graph complete. That is the argument made concrete: a bridge nobody cares about earns no payments and gets no investigation, and the first payments are what tell the newsroom where to dig. By the second year 41% of revenue comes from stories more than three months old, the twelve together earn £26,523 and £13,969 of profit, and across all of them the reporter earns £53 an hour.

[figure el-stories-chart.webp] Revenue by month across twelve stories: stories in their first three months in blue, the long tail of older stories in orange, which grows with every story added.

[figure collage-views-v3.webp] The vault, view by view: twenty of its twenty-three views, in the Day theme, the nine added in version 0.2 outlined.

**Costs and profit.** The fixed cost is mostly the reporting, and it comes first: 31 hours of the reporter's time and 4.5 of the editor's, both paid by the Courier, £1,350 with a legal read, set-up and the platform. Thirty-one hours is what the first week's payments justified: enough to dig into the contract and find the engineer, not enough to camp on the bridge, because an hour that does not pay for itself is an hour the next story needs. The variable costs, payments, alerts, compute and hosting, follow use and come to 9.3% of revenue. During the closure every party is in profit: the Courier makes £274 after paying her salary, the infrastructure share covers its costs with £20 to spare, and the reporter's top-up of £541 on a base of £930 comes to about £47 an hour against a base rate of £30. The story breaks even on 5 November, day twenty-five, and the scale chart says why the town mattered: below about 1,000 followers it would not have paid for its reporting, and above that every follower is margin.

**The next stories, and the payment as a signal.** The bridge is the first story in the Courier's graph, not the last. The vault plays out eleven more over two years: a school catchment change, the footbridge resurfacing, the county's sister-bridge inspections, a business rates review, a bus timetable, a wharf flood-defence overrun, a contractor's pattern across three councils, a car park, winter floods, a school meals contract and night closures on the bypass. Each starts with the council, the procurement portal, the routes and the contributors already in the graph, which saves 157 of 310 reporting hours. And each is sized by what people paid for in its first week, from readers and from institutions asking ahead: six are investigated, five get a tracker, and the footbridge resurfacing, which few people needed, gets a brief, an hour, and roughly breaks even. That is the argument made concrete: a bridge nobody cares about earns no payments and gets no investigation, and the first payments are what tell the newsroom where to dig. By the second year 41% of revenue comes from stories more than three months old, the twelve together earn £26,523 and £14,731 of profit, and across all of them the reporter earns £65 an hour, base and top-up together.

The money is also the bluntest editor in the building, and an honest one. Beside each story the vault records what the editor expected before the first week and what the town paid for. They agree on five of twelve. On four the town cared more, starting with the bridge itself, which the newsroom expected to be a week of roadworks; on three it cared less. A newsroom close to its community knows a lot about what matters to it, and the community, paying for what it needs, still knows more.

## Version 0.3: a professional finish, and the reporter in profit

The vault is also a demonstration of what a vault can be, so version 0.3 is a design and quality pass. The navigation is five numbered groups, the story, the people, the economics, the data and the vault itself, with an icon for each view, the three readers as people rather than indented lines, counts read from the data, and Previous and Next so the views read as a sequence. It has four themes, the same Night, Day, Paper and Ember as secrets.sgit.ai, with every colour a token valued in one file, so a theme is one block there and charts restyle in place.

[figure collage-themes-v3.webp] Four themes, one set of tokens: the same view in Night, Day, Paper and Ember.

Underneath, an architect agent reviewed the code against the estate's guidance, the vault-app rules on sgit.ai, coding.sgit.ai and nfrs.sgit.ai, and a developer agent applied it. Every view now renders through a template that escapes by default, so data in the vault cannot become markup; a view that cannot load its data says so instead of going blank; the interactive views keep keyboard focus; every chart has a text summary; and a gate of 44 checks, from the bundle contract and byte-for-byte downloads to theme completeness and contrast, fails the build if any of it regresses. The reviews and the decisions are in the vault, as `BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md` and `REALITY.md`.

The model was corrected in the same version, as described above: the reporter is on the Courier's payroll with a top-up from every use, the reporting was sized by the first week's payments, and every party ends the closure in profit. And beside each story, the vault now records what the editor expected against what the town paid for.

[figure el-editor-town-v3.webp] What the editor expected, and what the town paid for: five of twelve agreed; the town cared more about the bridge than the newsroom did.
